beats.intro: Chapter three, lesson three. Tertiary and quaternary structure. [[yarn]]A ball of yarn is one long thread folded into a shape. [[strip]]A protein folds the same way. Lesson two gave us the first two levels: the bead chain of amino acids, and its helices and sheets. [[lit]]Now we meet the last two: tertiary structure, and quaternary structure.
beats.tert: Start with one chain. [[parts]]Along it are stretches of helix, stretches of sheet, and loops in between. [[fold]]The chain bends and packs these pieces into one compact, three-dimensional shape. The final shape of a single chain is its tertiary structure. [[domain]]Your slide calls this folded shape a domain. Strictly, a domain is a compact region inside it, and a long chain may fold into several. [[fn]]The key point is the same either way. The shape decides the function, and if the shape is disrupted, the protein loses its activity.
beats.bonds: What holds the fold together? [[side]]This time the bonds join side chains, the R groups, not the backbone. [[hyd]]First, hydrophobic interactions. Non-polar side chains gather in the middle, away from water. [[hb]]Second, hydrogen bonds between side chains that carry polar groups. [[ion]]Third, ionic bonds, also called salt bridges, between a positive and a negative side chain. The slide spells it iconic, but it is ionic. [[ss]]And fourth, the disulfide bridge between two cysteines, the only covalent one. [[all]]Most of these are weak. Together, they lock the shape in place. [[out]]Notice where they sit. Hydrophobic side chains hide in the core, while charged and polar side chains face the water outside.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which bond is covalent?
beats.shape: Tertiary structures come in two broad shapes. [[ratio]]To tell them apart, divide the length of the molecule by its width. That is the axial ratio. [[glob]]A globular protein is compact, close to a ball. Its chain is tightly folded and coiled, and its axial ratio is under ten, about three to four. Insulin, the plasma albumins and globulins, and enzymes are globular. [[fib]]A fibrous protein is long, like a rope. Its chains are coiled in a spiral and held together by hydrogen bonds, and its axial ratio is over ten. Keratin, myosin, collagen and fibrin are fibrous. [[use]]The shape fits the job. Globular proteins tend to be the workers, like enzymes. Fibrous proteins give strength, in hair, nails and tendon.
beats.quat: Some proteins are made of more than one chain. [[subs]]Each chain is called a subunit, and each has its own primary, secondary and tertiary structure. [[pack]]Quaternary structure is how the subunits pack together into one closely fitting complex. [[bond]]They are held by hydrogen bonds, and by hydrophobic interactions between non-polar side chains. Ionic bonds often help too. [[one]]A protein with only one chain has no quaternary structure at all.
beats.ex: Three examples. [[ck]]Creatine kinase has two subunits, so it is a dimer. [[ldh]]Lactate dehydrogenase has four subunits, so it is a tetramer. [[hb]]Hemoglobin is a tetramer too: two alpha chains and two beta chains, each holding a heme group with an iron ion at its center. [[why]]Take hemoglobin apart, and no single chain does the whole job. The working protein is the complete group. [[count]]Two is a dimer, four is a tetramer.
beats.levels: Here is a question that mixes the levels. Which one holds each fold together? [[sec]]In secondary structure, hydrogen bonds join backbone atoms of one chain. [[ter]]In tertiary structure, four kinds of bond join side chains of one chain, and the disulfide bridge is the only covalent one. [[qua]]In quaternary structure, hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions join the surfaces of different chains. [[same]]So hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions appear again and again. What changes is where they act: backbone, side chain, or between chains.
beats.wrap: The four levels, in one picture. [[p]]Primary: the sequence of amino acids, joined by peptide bonds. [[s]]Secondary: helices and sheets, held by hydrogen bonds in the backbone. [[t]]Tertiary: one chain folded, held by bonds between its side chains. [[q]]Quaternary: several folded chains packed together. [[end]]Each level rests on the one below it. Now try the practice.
